name: Sanzhi Dargwa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Forker, Diana. 2020. A grammar of Sanzhi Dargwa (Languages of the Caucasus 2). Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3339225
catalog_locator: sect. 2.5 'Word stress', p. 30 (printed page number; PDF text)
catalog_quote: 2.5 Word stress. Stress is not a very prominent category in Sanzhi Dargwa. The stress is quite weak and the stress properties of words are very hard to determine, but they seem to be largely lexicalized. There are a few examples of minimal pairs or near minimal pairs that differ only in stress (31). (31) a. búk’ul ‘freezing’ b-uk’úl ‘thin, slender’ b. sːála ‘wedge’ salá ‘in front’ c. ákːʷar ‘without’ (postposition) akːʷár ‘not being’ (participle) d. hána ‘cast iron’ haná ‘now’. Some affixes attract stress, so that the position of stress in roots and in inflected word forms of one and the same lexeme may differ. For instance, plural suffixes of nouns normally attract stress (32). (32) a. qːap ‘sack’ > qːup-né ‘sack-pl’ b. kur ‘pit’ > kur-mé ‘pit-pl’. The factors influencing placement of stress require further research.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the LangSci PDF we hold/text at sect. 2.5, printed p. 30 (p. 50). (2) The deciding source is a 2020 open-access reference grammar by the language's principal fieldworker; Glottolog lists no phonology monograph or stress study for sout3261, and CrossRef/available web checks found no Sanzhi stress/prosody study (the 2026 Weirich et al. phonetic paper is on segmental/f0 gender variation). The 'lexical' coding with a morphological component (plural suffixes attract stress) follows directly from Forker's text, which itself flags the analysis as provisional ('require further research') — that hedge is a property of the state of knowledge, not of our sourcing. (3) The only structural caveat is scope: sout3261 is an umbrella languoid; grammars of Tanti (2014) and Icari (2003) exist and are not yet obtained. Second-hand evidence in the held Borise survey shows Tanti/Khudu

sources.citation: Yusupov, Kh. A. & S. M. Temirbulatova. 2025. Udarenie v darginskom jazyke, ego funkcii i leksikografičeskaja praktika [Stress in the Dargwa language, its functions, and lexicographic practice]. Filologija: naučnye issledovanija 2025(6): 82-91. DOI 10.7256/2454-0749.2025.6.74625 (open, CC BY-NC).
sources.quote: About literary (Aqusha-based, North-Central) Dargwa: 'даргинский литературный язык преимущественно характеризуется конечнослоговым фиксированным слабым ударением'; for southern varieties it reports distinctive, morphologically conditioned stress with accent-dominant affixes (Qaytag plural formants -bi, -ba, -ppi, -mi, -ti, -ni stressed; Tsugni/Sirhi 'существует небольшое число аффиксов, которые всегда несут ударение' incl. masdar -ni). Cites Forker 2020 and Sumbatova & Mutalov 2003 only for stress falling on long vowels. Does not treat Sanzhi itself.

sources.citation: Borise, Lena. [2018/2020]. Word stress in the languages of the Caucasus (ms./chapter; already held, not downloaded now:
sources.quote: No Sanzhi or Icari entry. For Tanti Dargwa (same Glottolog languoid): 'past forms of the verb systematically differ from participles in stress placement ... íxub throw.PRET, ixúb throw.PRET.PTCP (Lander & Sumbatova 2014: 123). In Tanti, many other verbal suffixes systematically attract stress too (Lander & Sumbatova 2014: 114)'; 'In Tanti Dargwa, some plural forms are derived by shifting the stress to the initial syllable (Lander & Sumbatova 2014: 50). Similarly, in Karbachimakhi, Khuduts and Nakhi Dargwa the initial syllable carries stress in plural forms (Shakhbanova 2010: 80).'

sources.note: Only dedicated cross-Dargwa survey of (nominal) stress, cited by Borise for which dialects have stress-attracting plural suffixes (p. 254) and free vs fixed stress (p. 266); would place the Sanzhi/South-western pattern in the family typology.

Establishes that sout3261 covers Amuzgu-Shiri, Sanzhi-Icari, Sirhwa-Tanty and Amukh groups and lists grammars: Sumbatova & Lander 2014 (752 pp, Tanti), Forker 2020 (620 pp, Sanzhi), Sumbatova & Mutalov 2003 (xv+257 pp, Icari), sketches Sumbatova 2020 (pp. 147-199 OUP Handbook) and Forker 2018 (30 pp).

sources.note: Icari is Sanzhi's closest sister (Sanzhi-Icari subgroup of sout3261) and Forker names this grammar as her model; its phonology chapter's stress section is the natural cross-check of 'largely lexicalized' + stress-attracting plural suffixes, and would show whether the classification holds beyond the Sanzhi doculect.
